desc:
Turn the string s into the string t using three kinds of operations, each applied to a single character:

  • insert any lowercase letter at any position, costing insertCost;
  • delete any character, costing deleteCost;
  • replace a character by a different letter, costing replaceCost.

Return the minimum total cost. Note that a replacement can be more expensive than a delete followed by an insert, in which case you should prefer the latter.

s = "kitten", t = "sitting", costs 1, 1, 1  ->  3
s = "abc",    t = "abd",     costs 1, 1, 5  ->  2   (delete c, insert d)
s = "ab",     t = "",        costs 1, 3, 1  ->  6
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Think about the last character of each prefix. What are the ways the prefixes s[:i] and t[:j] can end?
Let D[i][j] be the cheapest cost to turn the first i characters of s into the first j characters of t. The last step is a match (free), a replace, a delete of s[i-1], or an insert of t[j-1].
D[i][j] = min(D[i-1][j-1] + (0 if equal else replaceCost), D[i-1][j] + deleteCost, D[i][j-1] + insertCost), with D[i][0] = i*deleteCost and D[0][j] = j*insertCost. Only the previous row is needed.
editorial: Define D[i][j] as the minimum cost of turning the first i characters of s into the first j characters of t. Look at how the optimal sequence handles the last character of each prefix: the two last characters are matched together (free if equal, otherwise a replacement), or the last character of s is deleted, or the last character of t is inserted. That gives the three-way minimum above, and the boundary rows are all deletes or all inserts.

The costs only change the numbers inside the minimum, never the structure, so there is no need to treat 'replace is dearer than delete plus insert' specially: the table picks the cheaper route on its own. With a rolling row the memory is O(n). A greedy rule such as always replacing when lengths agree is wrong as soon as the costs are unequal.
